turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I’m your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: For about six weeks I’ve had tingling pain in the sole of my right foot, and it gets worse when I lift that leg higher during exercise. When I stop and rest a few minutes, the pain fully goes away, but I also get right calf cramps on treadmill incline that force me to break.
Doctor: When did the tingling pain in the sole of your right foot first start, and was there any specific event or activity that preceded its onset?

Patient: It started around six weeks ago, and I can’t point to a specific injury, but it seemed to begin after I started exercising more regularly about two months ago. The symptoms show up especially when I elevate my right leg during the workouts.
Doctor: Do you have any known medical conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol
Patient: Yes—I've had type 2 diabetes for about 8 years. I’m also a heavy smoker, but I don’t recall being told I have high blood pressure or high cholesterol.
Doctor: When you’re at rest, especially at night or when you’re sitting, do you notice any burning, numbness, or pain in your foot or calf that isn’t related to exercise?

Patient: At rest I mostly don’t have that tingling or burning, and it usually eases completely within a few minutes of stopping during exercise. Night or sitting doesn’t tend to cause the same symptoms in my right foot or calf.
Doctor: How far can you walk or run before the calf cramps and foot tingling start, and does the pain improve when you stop and rest, even if you stay upright?

Patient: It’s after a fairly predictable amount of walking on the treadmill—especially with the incline—when the right calf cramps start and the tingling in my sole shows up. If I stop and rest, the symptoms improve quickly and fully within a few minutes, and it helps even if I’m still upright and just pause the exercise.

Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in the color, temperature, or hair growth on your right foot or lower leg—such as the skin feeling colder, looking pale, or having less hair compared to the left side?

Patient: I haven’t noticed any major color change or that the right foot feels colder than the left, and I don’t recall any difference in hair growth down the leg. It’s mainly the tingling in the sole and the calf cramps that come on with the exercise incline or when I lift the leg. When I rest, both symptoms clear up within a few minutes.
Doctor: When you’re sitting or standing, can you feel the pulse in the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries of your right foot as easily as on the left, or is there any noticeable difference?

Patient: I haven’t specifically checked the pulses, so I can’t say whether they feel different on the right versus the left. If I did notice anything, it would be around the times when the calf cramps and sole tingling start during the incline exercise.
Doctor: Can you describe exactly where on the sole the tingling occurs—does it involve the heel, the arch, the ball of the foot, or specific toes?

Patient: It’s mainly along the arch and extending toward the ball of my right foot—more than the heel, and it doesn’t seem tied to just one toe. When the cramps start on the incline, the tingling follows in that same area.

Doctor: When you press gently on the inside of your ankle just behind the medial malleolus (the area of the tarsal tunnel), does that reproduce the tingling or cause any pain in the sole of your foot?

Patient: When I press that area behind the inner ankle, it does tend to reproduce the tingling in the arch and ball of my right foot, similar to what happens during the incline exercise. It’s not severe, but it feels like the same sensation.
[DDX] Tarsal tunnel syndrome, Peripheral diabetic neuropathy, Chronic exertional compartment syndrome of the calf
